694.title: The ache of missing God
694.hook: the gopis miss Krishna so much that the wise man sent to teach them learns bhakti from them
694.carry: missing God is a mark of bhakti
694.tomorrow: can you find something you never lost?
694.howItsDone: In many Vaishnava homes and temples, songs of longing for Krishna, often in the gopis' voice, are sung at evening aarti and in kirtan; poets call this love in separation viraha. Devotion also takes the other shapes the sutras name: daily puja, retelling the stories, and offering one's work to God.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and the opening of the Narada Bhakti Sutras: now, then, we will explain bhakti. The definition is supreme love.
screen: `PARAMA PREMA: SUPREME LOVE.`

segments.voice: Krishna has left the village of Vraja for the city of Mathura, and he hasn't come back. The cowherd women who loved him, the gopis, can't stop talking about him. So he sends his friend Uddhava, a wise and learned man, with a message: I was never really apart from you; turn your minds inward and you'll find me. Uddhava arrives to comfort them. In the Bhagavata Purana, he ends up being the one who's taught.
screen: `KRISHNA HAS LEFT VRAJA.` → `A WISE MAN SENT TO COMFORT.` → `HE ENDS UP BEING TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: The gopis hear the message, and they weep. One of them talks to a passing bee as if it were Krishna's messenger, half angry, half in love. They don't want a lesson; they want him. And Uddhava, the man of knowledge, is undone. He stays for months, and before he goes he says he'd gladly be a bush or a creeper in Vraja, just to be touched by the dust of those women's feet. Many teachers read it this way: knowledge came to teach love, and love taught knowledge. And a short Sanskrit book, the Narada Bhakti Sutras, points to the gopis as its example. Having defined bhakti as supreme love, it asks: what are its marks? Three teachers answer first. Vyasa: fondness for worship, the lamp and the flowers. Garga: fondness for the stories of the Lord. Shandilya: delight in the Self. Then Narada's own view: bhakti is offering every action to the Lord, and feeling deep anguish on forgetting him. The word is vyakulata: turmoil, the way a parent feels who loses a child in a crowd. Here's the teaching, one of Hinduism's most tender: missing God isn't a failure of devotion. It's one of its marks. Bhakti poets call love in separation viraha, and they've sung it for centuries. The sutras add one guardrail: even the gopis never forgot who Krishna was. So if your puja has slipped, many teachers would say the ache you feel isn't the door closing. It's the door.
screen: `THE GOPIS WEEP; A BEE GETS AN EARFUL.` · `UDDHAVA: LET ME BE A BUSH IN VRAJA.` · `FOUR TEACHERS, FOUR MARKS.` · `NARADA: ANGUISH ON FORGETTING.` · then, large: `MISSING GOD IS A MARK OF BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say one name of God you love, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, Devi, slowly, a few times, the way many Hindus do in japa. Between the names, notice any small ache of distance. Don't fix it; Narada counts it as love. If you don't pray, do the same with the name of someone you miss, and let the missing be what it is: a sign of how much they matter.
Bhakti. Devotion. Vyasa sees it in worship, Garga in the stories, Shandilya in delight, and Narada in the ache of forgetting. The gopis lived all four.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to this: missing God is a mark of bhakti. The gopis knew it. Day six hundred ninety-four, done.

695.title: The tenth man
695.hook: ten students count only nine, and a short poem of Shankara's says the Self is known, not earned
695.carry: the self is known, not earned
695.tomorrow: what's the one line under the whole year?
695.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta circles, the Atmabodha is often among the first texts a student reads with a teacher, verse by verse, alongside listening, reflection and meditation; teachers often tell the tenth man along the way. Many students pair study like this with work done as service and with devotion.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and Narada's mark of devotion, missing God is a mark of bhakti. The gopis missed Krishna, and taught a wise man love.
screen: `MISSING GOD IS A MARK OF BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Ten students cross a river in flood. On the far bank, their leader counts to be sure everyone made it. One, two, three, all the way to nine. He counts again: nine. Each of them takes a turn, and each one gets nine. So they sit on the bank and weep for the friend the river took. A traveler stops, listens, and asks the leader to count once more. Seven, eight, nine. And the traveler taps him on the chest: you are the tenth.
screen: `TEN CROSS THE RIVER.` → `EVERYONE COUNTS NINE.` → `YOU ARE THE TENTH.`

segments.voice: Advaita teachers have told that parable for centuries; Vidyaranya's Panchadashi uses it. Notice what the tenth man needed. Not a search party. Not more effort. Nothing was lost. He only had to know. That's the path of jnana, knowing, and a short Sanskrit poem called the Atmabodha, knowledge of the Self, puts it plainly. Tradition gives it to Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita Vedanta; some scholars question whether he wrote it. Advaita means not two: the deepest Self in you, the atman, and Brahman, the reality behind everything, are not two. The poem's second verse: as fire is what actually cooks the food, knowledge, not any other practice, directly brings freedom. Verse three gives the reason. Action isn't opposed to ignorance, so it can't destroy it. Knowledge is, the way light is opposed to darkness. Sweep a dark room all night; only a lamp ends the dark. And verse four: through ignorance the Self seems small; when ignorance goes, it shines on its own, like the sun when the clouds pass. So in this teaching you don't earn the Self, or build it, or fix it. It was never missing, any more than the tenth man was. That's the idea under the old line: you are not the body; you are atman. Not every school agrees on the road. Shankara's holds that knowledge alone frees, with action and devotion readying the mind. Ramanuja's tradition gives loving devotion to the Lord the central place, a knowing that has become love. Yesterday's gopis would like that.
screen: `NOTHING WAS LOST.` · `ADVAITA: ATMAN AND BRAHMAN, NOT TWO.` · `KNOWLEDGE FREES, AS A LAMP ENDS DARK.` · `LIKE THE SUN WHEN CLOUDS PASS.` · then, large: `THE SELF IS KNOWN, NOT EARNED.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let sounds, thoughts and feelings come and go. Then ask, quietly, the question Hindu teachers of self-inquiry give: who is noticing all this? Don't answer with a word. Just turn toward the one who's aware, the way the leader finally counted himself. If you drift, that's fine; noticing the drift is part of it.
Jnana. Knowing, from the root to know. Not collecting facts: seeing what was there all along, like the tenth man.
screen: `JNANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Take this with you: the Self is known, not earned. You were the tenth all along. See you tomorrow.

696.title: The seed of the banyan
696.hook: a father has his son break open a banyan seed and find nothing, and the whole year comes down to one line
696.carry: tat tvam asi: that you are
696.tomorrow: why does the greatest war story start with snakes?
696.howItsDone: Hindus often mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and the tenth man. The Self is known, not earned. Today, the last day of year two.
screen: `THE SELF IS KNOWN, NOT EARNED.`

segments.voice: A son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, isn't so sure. He points at a great banyan tree. Bring me one of its fruits. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? Tiny seeds. Break one of those. Done. What do you see now? The son, Shvetaketu, looks closely. Nothing at all, sir.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` → `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.`

segments.voice: This is the Chandogya Upanishad, where year two began. Uddalaka says: that fine essence you can't see, my son, out of it this whole great banyan stands. That finest essence is the Self of all that is. That is the real. And you are that, Shvetaketu. Tat tvam asi. It's counted among the great sayings of the Upanishads, the mahavakyas, and here's the teaching plainly: the deepest Self in you, atman, and Brahman, the reality behind everything, are not strangers. What you can't see holds up what you can. That line sits under this whole year. You heard Uddalaka again with salt dissolved in water: you can't see it, but every sip tastes of it. You heard Gargi pressing her questions. You read Patanjali defining yoga as the stilling of the turnings of the mind. You walked Valmiki's whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You kept a year of festivals. And this week, three paths: karma, bhakti, and jnana. Hindus don't all hear tat tvam asi the same way. Shankara's school hears it as one reality: you are Brahman. Ramanuja's hears the Lord living within you as your inner Self, inseparable from you, while you stay you. Both keep returning to this root. Year two was the root, and later teachers, and poets like Kamban and Tulsidas who retold Valmiki, keep coming back to it. Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a fire built for snakes.
screen: `AN ESSENCE TOO FINE TO SEE.` · `THE WHOLE BANYAN STANDS ON IT.` · `SALT, GARGI, PATANJALI, VALMIKI.` · `KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: If there's a seed nearby, a peppercorn, a mustard seed, a grain of rice, hold it in your palm. Somewhere in it, Uddalaka would say, is a whole plant you can't see. Then let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, the stilling of the mind, missing God is love, you are the tenth. Hold it on the breath, in on the first half, out on the second.
Mula. The root. The banyan stands on what you can't see, and later Hindu teachers keep returning to these roots: the Upanishads, Patanjali, Valmiki.
screen: `MULA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this: tat tvam asi, that you are. The branches come next. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

697.title: A story told beside a fire
697.hook: the Mahabharata begins with a king's fire for snakes, and the whole epic is told to him beside it
697.carry: itihasa: dharma learned from what happened
697.tomorrow: who put revenge in the king's ear?
697.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples the Mahabharata is heard more than read: a reciter or grandparent tells it in parts over many evenings, explaining as they go, and many families first met it through the televised serial. This year follows Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English translation, which is in the public domain.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka, a banyan seed, and the root of year two. Tat tvam asi, that you are. Today, year three begins.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: A forest called Naimisha. The sage Shaunaka and his companions are keeping a twelve-year sacrifice there. A traveler arrives: Ugrashravas, known as Sauti, the son of the storyteller Lomaharshana. They make him welcome and ask what anyone asks a visitor: where have you come from? From the snake sacrifice of King Janamejaya, he says, where he heard a great story told from beginning to end. The sages want all of it. So year three opens the way the Mahabharata opens: not on a battlefield, but in a forest, with someone asking for a story.
screen: `A FOREST, A SACRIFICE, A VISITOR.` → `WHERE HAVE YOU COME FROM?` → `A STORY HEARD AT A KING'S FIRE.`

segments.voice: This is the Adi Parva, the opening book of the Mahabharata, which year three follows a piece at a time, in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English. Before a single hero appears, it builds a frame. Sauti heard the story at King Janamejaya's sacrifice, told by Vaishampayana, a disciple of Vyasa; and Vyasa, the text says, composed the poem. Hand to hand, and now, through the book, to you. Janamejaya is the great-grandson of Arjuna, one of the Pandava brothers. His father, King Parikshit, died from the bite of Takshaka, a king of the snakes. So Janamejaya lit a great fire meant to draw every snake into the flames, and beside that fire, his family's whole war was told to him. That's why the greatest war story starts with snakes. Here's the teaching. The Mahabharata calls itself itihasa, usually explained as so indeed it was: not a rulebook, not a fairy tale, but what happened, told so you can watch dharma being kept and broken by real-seeming people. It even boasts, in its first book, about dharma, wealth, love and freedom: what is here may be found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere. And Hindus have mostly met it the way Janamejaya did: by hearing it, from a grandparent, a reciter, a TV serial, a teacher. Some readers hear the frame as a question the poem asks itself: what does a man in the middle of vengeance need to hear? Its answer is the story of where vengeance leads.
screen: `THE OPENING BOOK.` · `A FATHER, A SNAKE'S BITE.` · `A FIRE BUILT FOR REVENGE.` · `ITIHASA: SO IT WAS.` · then, large: `WHERE VENGEANCE LEADS.`

segments.voice: The Mahabharata opens with a bow: to Narayana, to Nara, and to Sarasvati, goddess of learning and speech, before the story is spoken. If you pray, make that small bow now, in your own words. Then just listen, to the room and the breath, for the rest of the sit. In Hindu learning, hearing, shravana, comes first. If you don't pray, bow your head to whoever first told you a story that mattered, and listen.
Adi Parva. The opening book of the Mahabharata, where the whole story is told beside a king's snake fire.

698.title: Uttanka's grudge
698.hook: a student loses a queen's earrings to a disguised snake king, and carries his anger all the way to Janamejaya
698.carry: krodha: anger is an enemy within
698.tomorrow: can one snakebite make every snake guilty?
698.howItsDone: Paying a teacher's fee at the end of study, guru dakshina, is a custom some Hindu students still keep, often as a gift or a service the teacher asks for. In the Adi Parva, Uttanka's journey ends at Janamejaya's court, and that is where the snake sacrifice begins to be urged.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Adi Parva opened beside a king's revenge fire. Itihasa: dharma learned from what happened. Today: who lit that fire?
screen: `ITIHASA: SO IT WAS.`

segments.voice: A student finishes his studies and asks his teacher what fee he can pay. The teacher sends him to ask his wife, and she names it: the earrings worn by the queen of King Paushya, brought back in time for a rite she means to wear them to. The student is Uttanka. The queen gives him the earrings, with a warning: Takshaka, the king of the snakes, wants them badly. Be careful. On the road home, Uttanka sets the earrings down to wash before his prayers. When he looks up, they're gone.
screen: `A STUDENT'S FEE.` → `A QUEEN'S EARRINGS.` → `SET DOWN, AND GONE.`

segments.voice: The beggar was Takshaka in disguise. He slips into a hole in the earth, down into the world of the snakes, and Uttanka follows. Down there it's like a dream: two women weaving with black and white threads, a wheel turned by boys, a man with a horse. The man tells him to blow into the horse; smoke and fire pour through the snake world, and a frightened Takshaka hands the earrings back. Uttanka pays his teacher in time. Done, you'd think. But he can't let it go. He travels to King Janamejaya and says: Takshaka killed your father. Avenge him. So the snake fire doesn't start with the king's grief alone. It starts with a student's grudge, carried a long way and set beside someone else's wound. Hindu teachers have a name for what's moving here. Anger, krodha, is one of the six enemies within, the shadripu: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Not enemies out there; enemies in here. And in the Bhagavad Gita, which sits inside this very epic, Krishna traces how anger travels: dwelling on something breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, blocked desire turns to anger, anger clouds the mind, and a clouded mind forgets what it knew. Uttanka was a good student. He'd won. But he kept dwelling, and his anger found a king with a bigger wound. Anger spreads like that, not always from the one who was hurt, but from the one beside them, saying: don't let this go. Next, a snake speaks up for mercy.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a grudge you were handed rather than one that began with you: a family feud, a friend's complaint, an old story about a whole group of people. Set it down in front of you, the way Uttanka set the earrings on the ground, and ask: whose was it first? Then notice where you are on Krishna's chain, dwelling, wanting, angry, clouded. Just see it, and breathe.

699.title: Ruru and the harmless snake
699.hook: a grieving groom vows to kill every snake he meets, until a harmless one speaks up and teaches him not to harm
699.carry: ahimsa: not harming is the highest dharma
699.tomorrow: who bets her sister's freedom on a horse's tail?
699.howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is taught in Hindu texts beyond this one, and some Hindus practice it through vegetarian diet, care for animals, and restraint in speech.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Adi Parva: Uttanka's grudge, carried all the way to a king. Krodha: anger is an enemy within.
screen: `KRODHA: ANGER IS AN ENEMY WITHIN.`

segments.voice: The wedding has been set. The bride, Pramadvara, is out with her friends, and she steps on a snake she doesn't see. It bites her, and she dies. The groom is Ruru, a young man of the family of the sage Bhrigu. He goes off alone into the forest and weeps. Then a messenger of the gods comes with an offer: she can live again, if he gives her half of his own life. He gives it. She wakes. They marry. It could end there, happily. It doesn't.
screen: `A BRIDE, A HIDDEN SNAKE.` → `HALF HIS LIFE FOR HERS.` → `IT DOESN'T END THERE.`

segments.voice: Ruru makes a vow: whenever he sees a snake, he will kill it. He carries a heavy stick and strikes the snakes he finds. One day he comes on an old snake of a kind called a dundubha, and he raises the stick. The snake speaks. I've done you no harm. Why strike me? A snake killed my wife, Ruru answers, so I kill snakes. The dundubha says: we're not the ones who bite. We share the name snake with them, and nothing else. Then it tells him who it really is: a sage, cursed to live in this shape until the day it met Ruru. Standing as a man again, the sage teaches him: not harming living beings is the highest dharma. Ahimsa paramo dharmah. A man of a priestly family should be known for gentleness and forgiveness, not for the stick. Notice where the Adi Parva puts this: inside the frame of a king trying to burn the snakes, a creature in a snake's shape speaks for ahimsa first. Ruru's grief was real. But he had turned one bite into a war on a whole kind of creature. That one phrase runs deep in Hindu life. It's a big part of why many Hindu families keep vegetarian kitchens, why a grandmother might carry a spider outside in a cup, and why ahimsa leads the list of restraints in the Yoga Sutras. The sage even points ahead and says Janamejaya's snake sacrifice was stopped. Then Ruru goes home to ask his father for the rest.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hurt that came from one person or one thing, and notice whether it has spread: from one dog to all dogs, one driver to all drivers, one person to everyone who looks like them. Don't argue with it; just see the line between the one that bit and the ones that never did. Breathe in on the one, and out on the many.

700.title: Kadru's bet and the nagas
700.hook: two sisters bet on a horse's tail, a mother curses her honest snake sons, and the epic still won't make snakes the villains
700.carry: the nagas are honored, not hated
700.tomorrow: a blazing egg cracks open. who's inside?
700.howItsDone: At Nag Panchami, in the rainy month of Shravan, many Hindu families offer milk, flowers and turmeric to images of the nagas, drawn on walls or shaped in clay or silver, and pray for protection. In the Adi Parva, Kadru's curse is the snakes' own family story: why the fire was coming for them.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Adi Parva: Ruru's stick, and a harmless snake who taught him. Ahimsa: not harming is the highest dharma.
screen: `AHIMSA PARAMO DHARMAH.`

segments.voice: What color is a white horse's tail? That's the bet between two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, both wives of the sage Kashyapa. They've just seen a marvelous white horse, Uchchaihshravas, which rose from the churning of the ocean. Vinata says the horse is white all over. Kadru says its tail is black. The stakes are steep: the loser becomes the winner's slave. They agree to go and look. Before they do, Kadru calls her sons. Her sons are snakes.
screen: `A WHITE HORSE FROM THE OCEAN.` → `A BET ON ITS TAIL.` → `THE LOSER BECOMES A SLAVE.`

segments.voice: Kadru tells them: go and hang on the horse's tail like black hairs, so I win. Some obey. Some refuse. And Kadru, furious, curses the ones who refuse: they will burn in the fire of a snake sacrifice held by a king named Janamejaya. That's the line the whole frame hangs on. The fire was spoken over these snakes long before Janamejaya was born. Brahma, the creator, hears the curse and lets it stand, because, the text says, the snakes had grown fierce and poisonous, a danger to others. The tail looks black, Vinata loses, and she serves her sister. And the curse fell on the innocent: the sons who said no to cheating. The text leaves that unease on the page. But a little later, the Adi Parva won't let the snakes be simple villains. They're children of a great sage, Kashyapa. Some refused to cheat. And Shesha, the eldest of them, turns from his brothers' cruelty toward Vinata, takes up austerities, and Brahma gives him a task: hold up the earth. In Hindu art, Vishnu rests on Shesha's coils on the cosmic ocean, and Shiva wears a snake at his throat. So Hindus don't only fear the nagas, the snake beings; many honor them. At Nag Panchami, families offer milk and flowers to images of the nagas and pray for protection. The same epic that builds a fire for snakes gives a snake the whole earth to carry.
screen: `THE SONS WHO REFUSE ARE CURSED.` · `BRAHMA LETS THE CURSE STAND.` · `THE CURSE FALLS ON THE INNOCENT.` · `SHESHA HOLDS UP THE EARTH.` · then, large: `THE NAGAS ARE HONORED, NOT HATED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a creature, or a kind of person, you've only ever seen as the threat. Now picture one of them like Kadru's sons who said no: doing the right thing at a cost. If you pray, offer that one a moment of honor, the way families offer milk and flowers to the nagas at Nag Panchami. If you don't, simply wish them well, once, on the out-breath, and let it rest.
